records.current_summary: Angola demands real caution from trans visitors. The 2020 Penal Code decriminalised same-sex conduct AND prohibited discrimination based on sexual orientation — one of Africa's stronger statutory packages on paper. A 2024 shadow report by Angolan LGBT organisations (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T and others) documents the gap: discrimination persists across health, education and employment; trans people have no legal gender recognition; and violence goes under-investigated. Luanda has a visible, organised community.

prison_adds.title: Human Rights Violations Against LGBTQI+ People in Angola — Shadow Report 2024 (Angolan CSOs; African Commission 81st session)
prison_adds.summary: Thin: the 2024 Angolan CSO shadow report (Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, Movimento T, ASTA and others) contains no data on where trans prisoners are housed in Angola — nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice. Closest documented finding: in June 2024 a transgender woman in Viana (Luanda) was attacked by police officers because of her gender identity, suffered physical injuries, was arbitrarily detained by Esquadra 43 and subjected to degrading treatment, with the case under investigation by the judicial military police of the Provincial Command of Luanda (police custody; no prison placement information). It also notes the 2020 Penal Code criminalises discrimination based on sexual orientation with up to two years' imprisonment.

records.current_summary: Antigua and Barbuda demands real caution. The High Court struck down the buggery/gross-indecency laws in July 2022, reading the constitutional bar on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity. No LGR, no anti-discrimination statute, and residual social hostility; tourist resort areas are insulated.

prison_adds.title: Antigua and Barbuda | Outright International
prison_adds.summary: Thin: Outright International country profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026'; fetched and subject-verified). The Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court's 2022 ruling struck down Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995, and read the constitutional bar on sex discrimination as inclusive of sexual orientation and gender identity; there are still no explicit anti-discrimination protections, same-sex unions are unrecognised, and transgender people are particularly vulnerable because no legal gender recognition mechanism exists. The profile contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement (birth-sex vs identity placement), special units, or solitary/segregation practice for Antigua and Barbuda.

records.current_summary:
Australia is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Gender identity has been a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act since 2013, and in August 2024 the Federal Court’s landmark Tickle v Giggle ruling confirmed that gender-identity discrimination protection covers trans women as women — with compensation awarded. States have modernised rapidly: Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections (April 2024) and NSW, another state, passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction; and marriage equality has held since 2017 (relevant to same-sex partners travelling together).

Counterweights: the Tickle case itself arose from organised exclusionary activism, which is vocal in Australia; ANROWS research documents systemic discrimination and harassment of trans people; and a NSW court granted a trans woman an apprehended-violence order against a Binary Australia activist who had targeted her — real harassment, but also functioning legal recourse.

For a visitor: full legal protection and functioning courts; low incident probability; border and document-screening practice is not detailed in the current sources.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison (Wikipedia; Australia section)
prison_adds.summary: Queensland placement policy: the 2009 Corrective Services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective (Jenny Samiec, Queensland Law Student Review 2009). Replacement oversight came via the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022 (fully in force 2023), whose August 2023 inspection standards for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally to be admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Staff still hold discretion at admission, and only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from that process - so Queensland placement is identity-based with a discretionary admission caveat and a surgery exception.

records.current_summary: Belize demands real caution. The Court of Appeal struck down the sodomy law in 2016 (Orozco v AG) — the Caribbean's first decriminalisation ruling; Belize has an organised community (UNIBAM) and anti-discrimination employment protection. No LGR; gang violence in Belize City is a general risk.

prison_adds.title: LGBTQ people in prison - Wikipedia
prison_adds.summary: Thin for Belize: the article (fetched, HTTP 200) surveys how LGBTQ prisoners worldwide are affected by strip-searching, solitary confinement, a disproportionate-incarceration risk, and transgender placement debates (including the US context), but its only Belize mention is a 'Violence in Belize' navbox taxonomy link. It contains no Belize-specific practice: no birth-sex-vs-identity housing rule, no trans special units, and no solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners in Belize; no usable placement finding.

records.current_summary:
Brazil combines some of the world's strongest legal protections for transgender people with a high level of real-world violence — the classic gap between law and practice. Courts allow name and gender-marker changes without surgery, the Supreme Court has criminalised transphobia (making it punishable like racism), courts fine businesses that discriminate, and official guidance affirms trans people's right to use bathrooms matching their identity.

For visitors, big-city queer life is vibrant and highly visible — São Paulo hosts the world's largest Pride parade — and the law is unambiguously on a trans traveller's side. The practical risks are concentrated in nightlife and app-based meetings: a majority of physical violence against LGBTQIA+ people in São Paulo happens at night, and robbery schemes luring gay men via dating apps have been fatal.

Exercise particular caution after dark, with nightlife and app meetings, and in peripheral areas. Violence against local trans people (Brazil records the world's highest absolute toll) is heavily concentrated in poor and marginalised communities, not tourist areas.

prison_adds.title: Resolução CNJ n. 348 de 13/10/2020 (alterada pela Resolução n. 366/2021) — diretrizes para o tratamento da população LGBTI custodiada ou privada de liberdade (Conselho Nacional de Justiça)
prison_adds.summary: Brazil's National Council of Justice (CNJ) Resolution 348 of 13 Oct 2020, as amended by Resolution 366 of 20 Jan 2021, is the national framework for where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed: a person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing (Art. 4º); on arrest, the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person is consulted about their preference (Art. 7º), and the judge must inform them of the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it general population or specific wings/cells (Art. 8º); the declared preference is recorded and a later change of placement is possible, with transfers prioritised in cases of violence or serious threat (Art. 9º). LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited (Art. 11, VI–VII). The resolution entered into force after publication (120 days, extended to 180 days by Res. 366/2021).

prison_adds.title: Elas também não são mulheres?: Travestis e mulheres transexuais em situação de prisão no Rio de Janeiro (Dilemas — Revista de Estudos de Conflito e Controle Social 17(2), 2024, e60615)
prison_adds.summary: Peer-reviewed census study (Alves-da-Silva & Bonan, Dilemas 17(2), 2024; lead author also of the LGBTI health division of the Rio de Janeiro state penitentiary administration, SEAP-RJ) of travestis and transgender women in prison in Rio de Janeiro state: 138 self-declared travesti/trans-woman inmates were interviewed inside eleven units deemed 'masculine' in the metropolitan region (April–June 2021, via the SEAP's SIPEN database). It documents that in the Rio state system travestis and trans women are housed in units treated as masculine, with some held in so-called 'neutral' or 'security' units, and frames male-unit placement as a double punishment combined with recurring basic-rights violations; it also cites the 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting them parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units (hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics) and national norms (2014; 2020) that let them be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.
